summary: Trevor found Duolingo's Thai lessons insufficiently practical for real-world communication while backpacking.
top_quotes: Duolingo's great if you're just muckin' around, but try orderin' a meal in a Bangkok street market with it—good luck, mate!
Learning a language ain't just about vocab, it's about sussing out how to get by when you're on the ground.
The app's fun and all, but when you're in the thick of it, you need more than just 'the cat drinks milk.'

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: G'day! How's it goin'? I'm Trevor, nice to have a chinwag about this language learnin' stuff.

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Right, so I'm Trevor, 23, from the land down under, Aussie born and bred. Always had the travel bug, so I took off backpackin' after school. Love the thrill of exploring new places, meetin' fresh faces, you know? Took a swing at learning Thai with Duolingo before my trip to Thailand, but, uh, didn't quite hit the mark, you could say.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grew up in Brisbane, you know, sunny Queensland. Bit of a relaxed spot, nice beaches, good vibes all around.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was pretty chill, mate. Brisbane's got that laid-back, beachy feel. Spent heaps of time outside, goin' to the beach, kickin' the footy with mates. Always somethin' to do, and the weather's beaut, so you can't really complain.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: I reckon a big turning point was when I decided to pack up and go backpackin'. Finished school and thought, 'Stuff it! I want to see the world.' Gave me a whole new perspective, really opened my eyes to different ways of livin'.

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Well, it just changed how I see things, you know? You step out of your comfort zone, meet people who live totally different lives, and it makes you think about what you really want. Plus, it's taught me to be more independent, really.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: Handled it by jumpin' in with both feet, really. Booked a one-way ticket and just started explorin'. Kept an open mind, stayed flexible, and just took things as they came. I think that's the best way to roll when you're on the road.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, I'm keen on just soakkin' up as much of the world as I can, you know? Travelling, learning new cultures, and meetin' new people. It's all about experiencin' life in all its weird and wonderful ways.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: It's important 'cause it makes you grow, doesn't it? You learn things you wouldn't otherwise, get a broader view of the world, and that can only be a good thing. Plus, it's about havin' stories to tell when you're old and grey.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day would be wakin' up somewhere new, explorin' a local market, tryin' weird foods, and endin' up chattin' with some locals over a cold beer. If I can learn a bit of the language along the way, even better.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: It's those moments where you feel like you’ve truly connected with the place and its people. When you go to bed thinkin', 'Yeah, that's why I do this,' that's a good day.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I kinda weigh it up in me head, but I go with my gut a lot. I reckon you know what feels right deep down. Talk with mates sometimes, see what they reckon, but at the end, it's gotta feel right to me.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Definitely go-with-the-flow, mate. Plans are great 'til they change, which they always do. You never know what's around the corner, so I'm all for just wingin' it.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Like when I was in Laos, planned to go north, but ended up meetin' some folks headed south to a lil' festival. Chucked in my plans, joined in with them, and had a ripper time. Sometimes the best experiences come from just bein' open to change.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: I try not to overthink it. I mean, life's full of risks, right? You can't bubble wrap yourself. So, I just dive in, think about the worst that could happen, and if I can live with that, then I'm good to go.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: Depends where I am, but usually it's breakfast at some local spot, bit of sightseein', maybe a hike or somethin'. I try to pick up bits of the language, chat with locals. Evenin's usually relaxin', watchin' the sunset, maybe a cheeky beer. It's laid-back but full, you know?

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: I reckon the constant travel, movin' from place to place. It can get a bit knackering, packin' up, sayin' goodbye to mates you've made. But it's part of the adventure, right?

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I guess I'd like more time to get deeper with the languages I'm tryin' to learn. You get a bit of survival speak, but I wish I could stick around and really get fluent, you know?

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Definitely been the budgets. Travelling’s expensive when you're goin' all over the shop, and you gotta watch how much you're spendin'. Can't always do everythin' you want, so you gotta be choosy.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I've learned to be frugal, look for deals on hostels, eatin' where the locals do, stuff like that. And workin' odd jobs to keep the funds topped up. You make it stretch, and you learn to enjoy the simple things.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: My family back home are a big part, always there for me. Then there's the mates I've met along the way, travel mates who become like a second family. Those connections are gold.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: It's like, even if we're miles apart, we can pick up right where we left off. We share a lot of experiences and look out for each other, like a proper family.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Right now, it's on the road, in hostels, or at local hangouts in the cities I visit. You get to see the world's livin' rooms, as I call 'em.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: Feel pretty free and alive, honestly. It's a tad chaotic but refreshing. There's always new things happenin', new stories unfoldin' around you.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: It's that unpredictability, you know? You never know what's comin' next, and that keeps life excitin'. It's the people, the cultures, always learnin' and experiencin'.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: First port of call is usually my family back home. They've got my back no matter what. And then the mates I've made on my travels, they're always good for advice and support.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: Oh, had a bit of a rough patch when I lost my wallet in Vietnam. Bit of a panic moment, no cash, no cards. Felt like the world's falling in, but you gotta keep a cool head.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: Taught me to be more careful with my stuff, that's for sure. But also showed me that people can be real kind—had a few mates lend me a hand 'til I got things sorted.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: Started by cancelling the cards quick smart, then contacted my folks to help sort some cash. Stayed with people I knew, did some work trades for a place to stay. You adapt and pull through.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: A breather and a good chinwag with someone who knows me. I tend to go for a walk, clear the head, and remind myself it's just a bump in the road.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: Hopefully still adventuring but with a bit more stability. Maybe have a base somewhere. I'd love to be fluent in a couple more languages and maybe even work in something that lets me keep travelin'.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I'd like to feel a bit more settled financially, you know? Enough so I can keep on the road but not worry about where the next meal's comin' from. A bit of security but still with the freedom.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before Duolingo, I was mostly doin' it the old-fashioned way. Grabbin' phrasebooks, askin' locals how to say things, watchin' stuff on YouTube. It was a bit hit and miss, to be honest. But you pick up a lot just by bein' pushed into it, you know?

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: Annoyin' part was definitely the time it took, right? You'd spend ages flippin' through books and still not have a clue when you tried to use it. And not always reliable stuff, missin' context and slang.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, first time in Bangkok, tryin' to order some food at a street stall. I had my phrases down from a book, thought I was hot stuff, but I butchered the pronunciation so bad, ended up with somethin' I didn't even order. Classic.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: Heard about Duolingo from a couple of backpackers I met in a hostel. They were all like, 'It's free, it's easy, give it a crack!' So I thought, why not, right?

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: The fact that it was free was a big seller, mate. Plus, everyone kept sayin' it was a bit of fun, like a game, so I figured it'd be a laugh and maybe I'd learn a thing or two.

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Alright, so last time I jumped on Duolingo, it was like, open the app and you're greeted with this cute little owl, right? Hit the Thai lessons and you're goin' through these levels, answerin' questions and tappin' pictures that match words. I like the bit where you repeat phrases, tryin' to mimic the accent. But it does feel a bit repetitive after a while, and you’re sayin’ stuff like ‘The cat drinks milk’ when you really need more practical chat. It’s fun but feels more like a game than actual conversing skills.

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: The pronunciation bits are tops. Helps you get your head around how things should sound. Pretty decent for drillin' in basic vocab too, like colours and numbers, which come in handy.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Ah, definitely the lack of context, mate. You finish a lesson and know a bunch of words, but stringin' 'em into a sentence in the real world, that's a whole different beast. The lack of practical phrases you actually use day-to-day is a bummer.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: It's how the lessons sometimes feel a bit random, like you’re learning words that you won't use much. It’s not quite geared towards actual conversation flow, which is what you need most when you're out there travelin'.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, this one time in Chiang Mai, tryin' to chat with some locals, realised all I could say were the basics and these random words. Couldn't keep up a convo. Felt a bit embarrassed, really. Made me wish I'd had more practical stuff under my belt.

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Yeah, I try to mix it up, you know? Use a bit of Duolingo to get the basics, then watch Thai YouTube vids or chat apps to hear real people speakin'. You gotta get used to slang and speed if you wanna keep up.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give you real-world chit-chat, mate. You start hearin' how people actually speak, not just textbook stuff. It's crucial for getting the rhythm and the feel of a language when you're out and about.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst-case? You end up spendin' heaps of time learnin' and still can't hold a basic conversation. Could leave ya stranded or missin' out on experiences 'cause you can't connect with local people.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I'm hopin' it's gonna give me useful phrases, help me remember stuff I actually need, and boost my confidence to speak when I'm out there. I want it to feel like I’m makin' real progress.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: It'd be when I can go into a cafe or a market, have a chat, and feel like I'm connectin'. When I can understand what someone says back to me without a blank stare on my face.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: If I could tweak it, I'd chuck in more real-life scenarios, you know? Conversations you'd actually have, like orderin' food, askin' for directions, not just talkin' about owls and cats.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: Reckon there should be more focus on cultural context and slang. It's not just about the words, it's how you use 'em and understanding the local lingo, right?

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: Nah, think we've hit all the big points. Just, maybe more encouragement for people to get out there and use the language in real life—like conversation meetups or exchanges.

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Uh, sure, why not? As long as it doesn't end up teachin' people to order milk-drinkin' cats in Thai, go for it!
